definitions.text: An electrophile (or electrophilic reagent) is a reagent that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from that reaction partner. An 'electrophilic substitution reaction' is a heterolytic reaction in which the reagent supplying the entering group acts as an electrophile. For example:  Electrophilic reagents are Lewis acids. 'Electrophilic catalysis' is catalysis by Lewis acids. The term 'electrophilic' is also used to designate the apparent polar character of certain radicals as inferred from their higher relative reactivities with reaction sites of higher electron density.

1. General Information 
 
Procedures employing oxygen - and/or moisture -sensitive materials were performed with 
anhydrous solvents ( vide infra ) using standard inert -atmosphere techniques (atmosphere of 
anhydrous dinitrogen). Analytical thin -layer chromatography was performed on precoated 
aluminium-backed plates (Silica Gel 60 F254; Merck), and visualized using a combination of UV 
light (254 nm) and acidic ethanolic vanillin, aqueous basic potassium permanganate or iodine 
stains. Preparative TLC was performed on precoated glass -backed preparative plates (Silica Gel 
15 F254; Analtech). Manual flash column chromatography was performed using Scharlab 60 silica 
gel (35-70 mesh); automated flash column chromatography was performed on disposable columns 
pre-packed with 50 μm spherical silica gel using a B üchi C-850 equipped with a UV-vis DAD 
(200-800 nm) and an ELSD detector. 
 
NMR spectra were recorded at 25 °C on a Bruker Avance 500 or 400 spectrometer (1H, 500 / 400 
MHz; 13C{1H}, 125 / 100 MHz; 19F NMR, 471 / 376 MHz). Chemical shifts are reported in ppm; 
coupling constants, J, are reported in Hz and are uncorrected for digitization. The follo wing 
abbreviations (and their combinations) are used to label the multiplicities: s (singlet), d (doublet), 
t (triplet), q (quartet), quint (quintet), sept (septet), m (multiplet) and br (broad).  1H and 13C{1H} 
chemical shifts are reported relative to tetr amethylsilane, and are referenced to the appropriate 
residual solvent peaks: 
 
• CDCl3: δH = 7.26 ppm, δC = 77.16 ppm 
• DMSO-d6: δH = 2.50 ppm, δC = 39.52 ppm 
• C6D6: δH = 7.16 ppm, δC = 128.06 ppm 
 
19F chemical shifts are reported relative to BF3•OEt2.  
 
Infrared spectra of neat compounds were recorded over the range 4000 -600 cm -1 using either a 
PerkinElmerSpectrum 1000 Series FTIR spectrometer with an ATR diamond cell, or a Bruker 
Alpha FTIR spectrometer fitted with a Bruker Platinum ATR Quicksnap™ diamond cell. Melting 
3 
 
points were measured using Stuart SMP10 or Gallenkamp melting point apparatus in open 
capillaries.  
 
High resolution electrospray ionization mass spectra (HRMS) were recorded using a Bruker ESI-
TOF MicroTOF II spectrometer.  
 
Reagent grade solvents (Fisher Technical) were employed. n-Hexane, MeCN, THF, toluene and 
Et2O were dried using an Inert PureSolv Grubbs -type system (alumina columns, argon 
atmosphere). CH2Cl2 was distilled from CaH2 under an atmosphere of anhydrous dinitrogen; DMF 
was distilled from 4 Å molecular sieved  under an atmosphere of anhydrous dinitrogen.  Unless 
stated otherwise, all reagents were used as received from commercial sources.

Organobismuth Compounds  
 
Tri(4-fluorophenyl)bismuthine 
 
A flame dried flask was evacuated and backfilled with anhydrous dinitrogen three times before 
magnesium turnings (4.01 g, 165 mmol) and ~3 iodine crystals were charged. The flask was heated 
until a purple vapour developed and stirred for 20 mins. Anhydrous THF (60  mL) was added 
followed by dropwise addition of 1 -bromo-4-fluorobenzene (17.0 mL, 155  mmol) at a rate that 
maintained reflux. The mixture was then stirred for 1 h, allowing time to cool to room temperature. 
In a separate flame dried flask under an atmosphere of N2, a solution of BiBr3 (22.4 g, 50.0 mmol) 
in anhydrous THF (75 mL) was prepared to which the Grignard reagent was added dropwise. The 
mixture was stirred for 1 h before quenching with water (100 mL), filtering through a pad of silica 
gel and extracting with Et2O (3  100 mL). The combined organic portions were dried over MgSO4 
and concentrated to dryness. Recrystallisation from hot ethanol afforded the title compound  
(22.2 g, 44.8  mmol, 90%) as a c olourless solid. Characterisation data were consistent with 
literature values. 1  
 
1H NMR (500 MHz, CDCl3): δH 7.66 (dd, J = 8.4, 6.2 Hz, 6H), 7.09 (app. t, J = 9.0 Hz, 6H). 
13C{1H} NMR (126 MHz, CDCl3): δC 163.0 (d, J = 247.3 Hz), 149.6 (br), 139.3 (d, J = 7.0 Hz), 
118.1 (d, J = 19.7 Hz).

the suspension of dilithiodiphenylsulfone via cannula over 20 mins at -78 °C. The resulting brown 
suspension was left to warm to rt over 18 h.

Procedure:  
A stock solution containing 4' -fluoro-1,3-dimethyl-[1,1'-biphenyl]-2(1H)-one 1a (0.10 M) and 
4,4'-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,1'-biphenyl (internal standard for 19F NMR spectroscopy; 0.0167 M) 
was prepared in the appropriate solvent. An aliquot (0.1 mL) was removed and diluted with CDCl3 
to confirm the initial ratio of the two compounds by quantitative 19F NMR spectroscopic analysis. 
For liquid additives: a flame dried flask was evacuated and backfilled with anhydrous dinitrogen 
three times before the stock solution (2.00 mL; 0.200 mmol of 4' -fluoro-1,3-dimethyl-[1,1'-
biphenyl]-2(1H)-one 1a and 0.0333 mmol of 4,4' -bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,1'-biphenyl) was added. 
The additive (1 equivalent) was then added via syringe before the reaction mixture was stirred at 
the given temperature. 
For solid additives: a flame dried flask containing the additive (1 equivalent) was evacuated and 
backfilled with anhydrous dinitrogen three times before the stock solution (2.00 mL; 0.200 mmol 
of 4' -fluoro-1,3-dimethyl-[1,1'-biphenyl]-2(1H)-one 1a and 0.0333 mmol of 
4,4'-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,1'-biphenyl) was added and the mixture was stirred at the given 
temperature. 
Aliquots (0.10 mL) of the reaction mixtures were removed at given times and added to water (0.1 
mL). The organic layer was separated, diluted with CDCl 3, and analysed by 19F NMR 
spectroscopy. 
 
Commentary:  
Entry T was initially selected as the preferred conditions for the 1,2-aryl migration / 
rearomatization. However, yields proved inconsistent when these conditions were applied to other 
substrates; in contrast, the conditions described in entry F proved more general and were therefore 
employed in subsequent studies.  
Acid-sensitive cyclohexadienones ( e.g., 20a, 21a) proved incompatible with the conditions of 
entry F. While 1,2-aryl migration was not promoted by TMSOTf in the presence of base, led to no 
(entry W), quantitative 1,2-aryl migration was observed in the presence of Bi(OTf)3 / NEt3 (entry 
X). These conditions were therefore employed for any potentially acid-sensitive substrates.

Substrate Scope (Manuscript Table 1) 
General Procedure 1 – Synthesis of Cyclohexadienones  
 
A mixture of 5,5-dioxido-10H-dibenzo[b,e][1,4]thiabismin-10-yl 4 -methylbenzenesulfonate S1 
(596 mg, 1.00 mmol), NaHCO3 (92.4 mg, 1.10 mmol), and arylboronic acid (1.10 mmol) in toluene 
(10 mL) and H2O (0.50 mL) was stirred at 60 °C until starting material was no longer observed by 
1H NMR spectroscopy. The reaction mixture was cooled to rt before aq. NaOH (2.0 M; 2 mL) was 
added and vigorously stirred for 5 mins. The organic  phase was removed, and the remaining 
aqueous portion was extracted with toluene (2 mL). The combined organic portions were filtered 
through a pad of MgSO 4 (1 cm3) into a round-bottom flask containing the phenol substrate (1.00 
mmol). The mixture was stirred as mCPBA (89% purity; 194 mg, 1.00 mmol) was added portion-
wise over 5 mins and left to stir for a further 30 mins.  
Saturated aq. Na2S2O5 (1 mL) was then added and stirred for 5 mins before the solution was diluted 
with water (20 mL) and extracted with EtOAc (20 mL). The organic portion was washed with sat. 
aq. Na2CO3 (2 × 10 mL), before the aqueous layers were combined and extracted with EtOAc (3 
× 10 mL). The organic portions were combined, dried over MgSO4, filtered, and the volatiles were 
removed under reduced pressure. The crude product was purified by silica gel column 
chromatography using the eluent system described for individual compound entries. 
  
43 
 
General Procedure 2 – 1,2-Aryl Migration / Rearomatization 
 
A flask containing the cyclohexadieneone was evacuated and backfilled with anhydrous dinitrogen 
three times. Anhydrous toluene ([cyclohexadieneone]0 = 0.10 M) was added and the solution was 
cooled to 0 °C before trimethylsilyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (1 .0 eq.) was added dropwise via 
syringe over 5 mins and left to warm to rt over 18 hours. Sat. aq. NaHCO3 (5 mL) was added and 
stirred for 15 mins before the aqueous layer was removed and extracted with EtOAc ( × 3). The 
combined organic  portions were dried over MgSO 4, filtered, and concentrated under reduced 
pressure. Where further purification was required, the appropriate procedure is described for 
individual compound entries.

Discussion of the Mechanism and Regioselectivity of Bi(V)-Mediated Arylation 
 
Bismuth(V)-mediated arylation of phenols is generally accepted to proceed via an EAS-like ligand 
coupling mechanism14 in which the aryl-Bi(V) moiety acts as a C-electrophile that is attacked by 
the nucleophilic phenol. Radical pathways have been ruled out experimentally by EPR and radical 
trapping experiments ,15,16 and computationally in analogous Bi(V) -mediated C -O bond 
formation.17 Nonetheless, it is important to rule out an alternative mecha nism based on two-
electron oxidative coupling – common in other high valent element chemistry18,19 – in which Bi(V) 
oxidises the phenol to a transient phenoxonium cation th at is then trapped by a nucleophilic aryl-
Bi(III) ‘ate’ species. In the following discussion, we present additional experimental data that 
support operation of the ligand coupling mechanism. 
 
Substrate synthesis is presented in Supplementary Section 2 (“ Substrates for Additional 
Mechanistic and Regioselectivity Studies”). 
 
Kinetic Isotope Effects on Arylation. The dearomatisation of d3-2,6-dimethyl phenol to form d3-
1a occurs without an appreciable kinetic isotope effect (manuscript Figure 4b; see Supplementary 
Section 5 for details). The absence of a β -SKIE is consistent with a concerted EAS -type ligand 
coupling mechanism, and not with intermediacy of a phenoxonium cation in the selectivity 
determining step. For a reaction proceeding via a carbocationic intermediate, a β -SKIE of ca 1.1 
is expected per deuterium due to the differences in hyperconjugative stabilisation afforded by the 
C-H and C -D bonds. For example, oxidation of para-xylene to its rad ical cation, 20 step-wise 
cycloaddition of PTAD21 or TCNE22 with alkenes, and the equilibration of β-halocarbenium ions23 
all exhibit non -zero β -SKIEs, consistent with reaction via carbocationic intermediates. On the 
other hand, no β -SKIE is observed for reactio ns that do not proceed via a kinetically relevant 
carbocation, such as: dearomatisation of anthracene via [4+2] cycloaddition, 24 epoxidation of 
alkenes with DMDO25 or mCPBA,26 or concerted [4+2] cycloadditions.27 As such, the fact that we 
do not observe a KIE in the formation of d3-1a indicates that a phenoxonium intermediate is not 
involved in the arylation, and instead suggests that the regioselectivity of arylation is determined 
via a pathway that does not develop full positive charge at either ortho position of the phenol. 
96 
 
Regioselectivity of Arylation. In additional studies, we have demonstrated that nonsymmetrical 
meta-terphenols of the type  2-(4-fluorophenyl)-6-(4-X-phenyl) phenol are arylated ipso to the 
more electron-rich aryl substituent (Supplementary Figure 1; ρ+ = -0.33, r2 = 0.97).

Discussion of Atom Economy 
 
(1) Arylating agent.  The use of stoichiometric boronic acid is require d as 1 equivalent of aryl 
moiety must be delivered to the phenol. Where we use just 1.1 equivalent s of boronic acid, 
competing methods are typically less economical. For example, considering ortho-selective 
arylations that are broadly comparable to our Bi(V)-mediated method:  
- Barton reports use of [Ph 4Bi]X or BiPh 5, ultimately requiring 4 or 5 equivalents of aryl 
moiety.29,30,31  
- Single-electron ‘oxidative-couplings’ typically require 3-10 equivalents of arene.32,33,34,35  
Considering extant methods for the direct meta-selective arylation of phenols: 
- Yu’s templated arylation employs 3 equivalents of arylboronic ester.36 
- Yu’s Catellani-type arylations employ 237 or 338 equivalents of aryl iodide. 
- Larossa’s traceless directing group strategy employs 3 equivalents of phenol (i.e., reversed 
stoichiometries of coupling partners).39 
(2) Bismuth. The bismuth reagent is used in stoichiometric quantities but, as detailed above, can 
be recovered in 94% yield simple precipitation . This equates to loss of just 6 mol% Bi reagent, 
making it comparable to catalytic meta arylation protocols that use 2-15 mol% Pd catalyst with 
Ag salts as terminal oxidants (neither of which are recovered).36,38,39,37 
(3) Oxidant. The use of 1.0 equivalent of mCPBA as a stoichiometric oxidant in our methodology 
is comparable or  preferable to the (excess) silver salts employed in competing meta-selective 
arylation strategies.36,38,39,37 
(4) Lewis acid.  While we use stoichiometric TMSOTf to induce 1,2 -aryl migration / 
rearomatisation for the majority of the substrate scope, we also demonstrate that catalytic amounts 
of Bi(OTf)3 can be used to effect the same transformation.
